back: Bipedalism and the associated skeletal changes, increasing cranial capacity, reduced prognathism and dentition, and the use of these features to interpret hominin fossils.

points.area: Unit 4: How does life change and respond to challenges? — AoS 2: How are species related over time?
points.title: Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and human migration
points.detail: Evidence for the out-of-Africa model, comparisons between Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis, and evidence of interbreeding from Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA.

questions.q: Describe two lines of evidence that support the out-of-Africa model of modern human origins.
answer: The oldest Homo sapiens fossils are found in Africa, with progressively younger fossils found further from Africa.
Genetic diversity is greatest in African populations, consistent with a longer period of accumulated mutation there.
Mitochondrial DNA and Y chromosome lineages of modern populations trace back to African ancestors, while Neanderthal DNA in non-African genomes indicates later interbreeding during migration.

points.area: Unit 4: How does life change and respond to challenges? — AoS 3: How is scientific inquiry used to investigate cellular processes and/or biological change?
points.title: Designing the investigation
points.detail: Selecting a question within a designated topic, developing an aim and hypothesis, choosing a methodology and planning a repeatable method with appropriate controls.

questions.q: Outline three decisions that must be made when designing a controlled experiment, and explain why each affects the validity of the results.
answer: Choosing which variable to manipulate and which to measure determines whether the investigation actually tests the hypothesis.
Deciding which variables to control prevents extraneous variables from confounding the results.
Choosing the number of trials and the sample size affects how well random error and individual variation are accounted for.

card.title: Designing the investigation
back: Selecting a question within a designated topic, developing an aim and hypothesis, choosing a methodology and planning a repeatable method with appropriate controls.

points.area: Unit 4: How does life change and respond to challenges? — AoS 3: How is scientific inquiry used to investigate cellular processes and/or biological change?
points.title: Logbook, safety and ethics
points.detail: Maintaining a logbook as an authenticated record of planning, changes and raw data; risk assessment; ethical considerations for organisms and participants.

questions.q: Explain why a logbook is required and what should be recorded in it if a method is changed part-way through an investigation.
answer: The logbook is an authenticated primary record that allows the work to be verified and reproduced.
Any change to the method must be recorded with the date and the reason for the change.
Data collected before and after the change must be clearly distinguished so that results are interpreted correctly.

card.title: Logbook, safety and ethics
back: Maintaining a logbook as an authenticated record of planning, changes and raw data; risk assessment; ethical considerations for organisms and participants.

points.title: Generating and recording data
points.detail: Collecting primary quantitative and qualitative data, choosing appropriate units and precision, and organising raw data into tables with headings and units.

questions.q: State two features of a well-constructed results table and explain why each is needed.
answer: Column headings include the quantity and its unit, so readers can interpret the values without ambiguity.
Values are recorded to a consistent number of decimal places reflecting the precision of the instrument.
Raw data and processed values such as means are shown separately so calculations can be checked.

card.title: Generating and recording data
back: Collecting primary quantitative and qualitative data, choosing appropriate units and precision, and organising raw data into tables with headings and units.

points.title: Analysing and evaluating results
points.detail: Identifying trends and relationships, distinguishing correlation from causation, evaluating the accuracy, precision, repeatability and validity of the method, and suggesting improvements.

questions.q: An investigation produced results that broadly matched the hypothesis but had a large spread between trials. Evaluate this outcome and suggest one improvement.
answer: The large spread indicates low precision, most likely caused by random error in measurement or uncontrolled variation between samples.
The conclusion can still be supported, but with reduced confidence, and the limitation must be stated.
Increasing the number of trials and tightening control of extraneous variables would reduce the spread.

card.title: Analysing and evaluating results
back: Identifying trends and relationships, distinguishing correlation from causation, evaluating the accuracy, precision, repeatability and validity of the method, and suggesting improvements.

points.title: Communicating with a scientific poster
points.detail: The structure of a scientific poster including title, introduction, methodology and method, results, discussion and conclusion, and conventions for referencing and figures.

questions.q: State what belongs in the discussion section of a scientific poster, and how it differs from the conclusion.
answer: The discussion interprets the results, links them to the hypothesis and relevant biology, and evaluates limitations and sources of error.
The conclusion is a brief statement of what was found in relation to the aim, without new interpretation.
The discussion may also suggest further investigations; the conclusion should not introduce information not supported by the results.
